Nearly two-thirds of marketers claim at least 75% of their translated or localized web content is translated by a machine translation engine in a normal month.
In a normal month, 42% of marketers use machine translation to translate 51–100 million characters, while 39% use it to interpret 101–500 million characters a month.
Most marketers employ human review and editing after using machine translations, and three in ten (30%) do it all the time.

Overall, nearly nine out of ten marketers (87%) say it is easy to translate their website content into multiple languages, with more than half (55%) saying it is somewhat easy and one-third (32%) saying it is very easy.
Almost 90% of marketers think that translating material into multiple languages can be both expensive and hard.

Seven out of ten (69%) say that the overall cost of the work is frustrating when it comes to content translations, and more than two-thirds (68%) say that the number of people participating in the whole process is frustrating.
Also, two-thirds of marketers find it frustrating that there are technical problems with putting the translated content on the website (67%) and that it takes a long time (66%).
Nearly two-thirds of marketers find it frustrating to work with IT and/or the tech staff (65%), SEO for their translated content (64%), and external firms or vendors (64%).
Over one-fifth of marketers (22%) say that working with IT and/or tech staff is their biggest frustration when it comes to translating content.
Almost one-fifth (18%) say that technical challenges with publishing the translated content on the website are their biggest frustration.
Less than one-fifth (16%) say that the number of people who must be involved in the end-to-end process and SEO for their translatable content is their biggest frustration.
More than one in ten (13%) say that the overall cost of the project is the thing that bothers them the most.
Working with outside agencies or companies (7%) and the overall length of the project (7%) come in second and third, respectively.
Over two-fifths of Japanese marketers (43%) say working with IT and/or technical staff is their biggest frustration.

One-quarter of French marketers (24%) say SEO for their translated content, more than one-fifth of American marketers (22%) say technical problems with putting the translated content on the website, and one-fifth of German marketers (20%) say SEO for their translated content and the overall cost of the work are their biggest frustrations, respectively.
Almost nine out of ten marketers (87%) agree that machine translation is an important tool for localization and translation projects.
In fact, nearly all marketers (98%) say they use machine translation for their content.
One-quarter (24%) use it constantly, and more than half (53%) use it often.
Nearly two-thirds of marketers (64%) say that at least 75% of the web content they translate/localize each month is translated in whole or in part by a machine translation tool.
Over 80% of French marketers, about 70% of Japanese marketers, and about 68% of German marketers use machine translation for at least 75% of their website content.
But slightly more than one-third of American marketers (36%) say the same thing, and more than two-fifths (44%) say that machine engines translate about 25% of their web content.

Over two-fifths of marketers (42%) say they use machine translation to translate 51-100 million characters in a normal month, and two-fifths (39%) say they use it to translate 101-500 million characters.
Machine translation is more likely to be used for 101-500 million characters per month by French and German marketers than by Japanese and American marketers (65% vs.
26% & 17%, respectively).
Almost three out of five marketers (57%) use machine translations/localizations for product information.
Half use it for company information (50%) and user-generated content (49%), and more than two out of five use it for news stories (45%) and blog posts (44%).

Over four out of five marketers say that when they use machine translation, the accuracy of the text suffers (83%), they worry about data security (83%), the creative tone is lost (82%), and product- or industry-specific jargon is not translated correctly (82%).
They also say that context and/or nuance are lost (79%) and corporate phrases are not handled correctly (79%).

When it comes to product, company, or industry terms that must be translated in a certain way, one-third of marketers usually have human editors change the machine-translated results (34%), and they train their own custom machine translation models (33%), while more than one-quarter (28%) use a glossary function provided by the machine translation vendor.
Nearly all marketers (99%) say they use human review and/or rewriting when using machine translations.
One-third (30%) do this always, and more than half (54%) do it often.
Over 80% of those who answered, however, wish that their localization and translation projects did not need as much human review and rewriting.
After this human review, more than four in five (85%) say the translation needs to be changed.
One-third (30%) of marketers say it needs to be changed significantly, and more than half (55%) say it needs to be changed significantly.
After the human review, more than nine out of ten marketers in France (95%) and Japan (94%), but only three out of four in Germany (76%) and the US (74%), think the language needs to be changed.
And almost all marketers (98%) are happy with how human judges usually edit translated content, but only a little more than a third (37%) are very happy.
But only 86% of marketers think they wouldn't be able to translate their content on budget if they didn't have machine translation.
In terms of return on investment (ROI), only 4% of marketers think that the money they make from their translation/localization projects is the same as or less than what the projects cost.
Three out of ten marketers report a return on investment of 2X (29%), 4X (29%), 3X (27%), 5X (9%), or 3X (9%).

Over nine out of ten marketers say that accuracy and/or quality (93%), support (93%), data security and privacy (93%), cost (93%), having an API (93%), being able to add company or industry vocabulary (93%), performance (93%), and support for all their key languages (92%) are important when choosing a machine translation tool.

When asked which two things are most important to them when choosing a machine translation tool/vendor, almost a quarter (23%) say the ability to handle XML, HTML, and/or specific document formats is most important, while one in five say data security and confidentiality (20%), the tool offers an API (20%), and customizability (19%) are.

Less than one-fifth of respondents say that accuracy and/or quality (16%), performance (16%), and case studies that show similar projects or companies (15%) are most important, while smaller numbers say that support availability (14%), cost (14%), support for their primary languages (14%), and ease of use (11%).
One-third of Japanese marketers (33%) say that being able to handle XML, HTML, and/or specific document formats is their top priority.
On the other hand, one-third of French marketers (29%) say that the vendor's product plan and recent product improvements are their top priorities.
More than a quarter of German marketers (27%) say that help is the most important thing when choosing a machine translation tool.
On the other hand, one quarter of American marketers (26%) say that data security and privacy is the most important thing.
Over two-fifths of marketers (44%) work with a technology partner that uses the machine translation/localization vendor.
One-third of marketers work with a firm that uses the machine translation vendor, and almost one-quarter (23%) work directly with the machine translation vendor.

96% of respondents report a positive ROI on their translation/localization projects, with 65% reporting an ROI of 3x or greater.

77% of respondents are using AI assisted writing to generate content, with the majority (98%) believing a large amount of content will be AI generated in the next 2-3 years Generative AI isn't going away any time soon, and, rather than a gimmick or tech demo, marketers are using commercial AI tools to augment their workflows.
82% of respondents report that product, company or industry vocabulary jargon is not translated accurately when only using machine translation.

Overall, almost nine in ten marketers (87%) say translating their web content into multiple languages is easy, but over half (55%) say it is somewhat easy and just one-third (32%) say it is very easy.
Almost nine in ten marketers say having to translate content into multiple languages can be costly (87%) and can be difficult to do (87%).
Over four in five (82%) say translating content correctly can be frustrating.

Specifically with regard to frustrations, seven in ten (69%) say the overall cost of the work is frustrating when it comes to their content translations, over two-thirds (68%) say the number of people that need to be involved in the end-to-end process is frustrating and two-thirds of marketers say technical challenges with publishing the translated content on the website (67%) and the overall time it takes (66%) are frustrating.

Almost two-thirds of marketers say, when it comes to their content translations, having to work with IT and/or the tech staff (65%), SEO for their translated content (64%) and having to work with external agencies or vendors (64%) are frustrating.

With all of these issues being frustrations, when asked which one is most frustrating, over one in five marketers (22%) say having to work with IT and/or tech staff is their greatest frustration when it comes to their content translations, almost one in five (18%) say technical challenges with publishing the translated content on the website and less than one in five say the number of people that need to be involved in the end-to-end process (16%) and SEO for their translated content (15%) are the greatest frustrations.

Over one in ten (13%) say the overall cost of the work is their greatest frustration and almost one in ten say it is having to work with external agencies or vendors (7%) and the overall time it takes (7%).

Over two in five Japanese marketers (43%) say having to work with IT and/or technical staff is their greatest frustration, one-quarter of French marketers (24%) say it is SEO for their translated content, over one in five American marketers (22%) say it is technical challenges with publishing the translated content on the website and one in five German marketers each say their greatest frustration is SEO for their translated content (20%) and the overall cost of the work (20%).
Almost nine in ten marketers (87%) agree that machine translation is an indispensable tool for localization/translations projects.
In fact, just about all marketers (98%) say they use machine translation for their content with one-quarter (24%) using it all the time and over half (53%) using it most of the time.

Specifically looking at their web content, almost two-thirds of marketers (64%) say, in a typical month, at least 75% of their web content that they translate/localize is partially or fully translated by a machine translation engine.
Over four in five French marketers (83%) translate at least 75% of their web content by a machine engine as do around seven in ten Japanese (69%) and German (68%) marketers.
However, just over one-third of American marketers (36%) say the same while over two in five (44%) say they translate about 25% of their web content by machine engine.

For how much they translate, over two in five marketers (42%) say, in a typical month, they use machine translation to translate 51-100 million characters while two in five (39%) say they use it to translate 101-500 million characters.
French and German marketers are more likely than Japanese and Americans to say they use machine translations for 101-500 million characters a month (65% & 50% vs.

When it comes to the type of content translated by machine, almost three in five marketers (57%) use machine translations/localizations for product information, half use it for company information (50%) and user-generated content (49%) and over two in five use it for news articles (45%) and blog posts (44%).
Among those who use machine translations for user-generated content, three-quarters (74%) have integrated a machine translation engine directly with internal tooling.

Machine translations aren’t perfect and over four in five marketers say, when using machine translation, the accuracy of the text suffers (83%), there is concern about data security (83%), creative tone is lost (82%) and product- or industry-specific jargon is not being translated accurately (82%) while four in five say the context and/or nuance is lost (79%) and corporate phrases are not handled correctly (79%).

Specifically when it comes to product, company or industry vocabulary that needs to be translated a specific way in their machine translation projects, one-third of marketers normally have human editors modify the machine translated results (34%) and they train their own custom machine translation models (33%) while over one-quarter (28%) use a glossary feature provided by the machine translation vendor.

When they use machine translations, just about all marketers (99%) say they follow it up with human review and/or editing with three in ten (30%) doing so all the time and over half (54%) doing so most of the time.
But, over four in five (84%) say they wish they did not need so much human review and editing with their localization/translation projects.
After that human review, over four in five (85%) say the translation needs to be changed with three in ten marketers (30%) saying a lot of it does and over half (55%) saying a good deal of it does.
Over nine in ten marketers in France (95%) and Japan (94%) say the translation needs to be changed after the human review compared to three-quarters of those in Germany (76%) and the US (76%).
And, overall, while almost all marketers (98%) say they are satisfied with the job the human reviewers typically do editing translated content, just over one-third (37%) are very satisfied.
But, less than nine in ten marketers (86%) say without machine translation, they are not sure they would be able to stay on budget with their content translations.

Over four in five marketers say machine translation can be cheap now, but expensive later when editing (83%) and they would have a better return on their investment in machine translation if their human reviewers did not have to edit as much (83%).
Looking at ROI, very few marketers (4%) estimate that, on their translation/localization projects they generate as much as or less revenue than the project costs.

Three in ten marketers each say they generate 2X ROI (29%) and 4X ROI (29%), over one-quarter (27%) say they generate 3X ROI and one in ten marketers (9%) say their translation/localization projects generate 5X or more ROI.

When it comes to selecting a machine translation tool, over nine in ten marketers say accuracy and/or quality (93%), the support available (93%), data security and confidentiality (93%), cost (93%), that the tool offers an API (93%), customizability, that is the ability to incorporate company or industry vocabulary (93%), performance, that is how long it takes to receive the machine translations (93%) and support for all their key languages (92%) are important to them.

Nine in ten say the vendor product roadmap and recent product improvements (91%), case studies featuring similar projects or companies (91%), the ease of use (90%) and the ability to handle XML, HTML and/or specific document formats (89%) are important to them.

With all of these important to marketers, when asked to select which two are most important to them when selecting a machine translation tool/vendor, almost one-quarter (23%) say the ability to handle XML, HTML and/or specific document formats is most important while one in five say data security and confidentiality (20%), the tool offers an API (20%) and customizability (19%) are while almost one in five (17%) say the vendor’s product roadmap and recent product improvements is most important.

Less than one in five say accuracy and/or quality (16%), performance (16%) and case studies featuring similar projects or companies (15%) are most important while smaller numbers say the support available (14%), cost (14%), the support for their key languages (14%) and the ease of use (11%) are most important.

One-third of Japanese marketers (33%) say the ability to handle XML, HTML and/or specific document formats is most important to them while three in ten French marketers (29%) say the vendor’s product roadmap and recent product improvements is most important.

Over one-quarter of German marketers (27%) say the support available is most important while one-quarter of American marketers (26%) say, when selecting a machine translation tool, data security and confidentiality is most important.

When it comes to working with a machine translation/localization vendor, over two in five marketers (44%) say they normally work with a technology partner that uses the machine translation vendor, one-third (33%) work with an agency that uses the machine translation vendor and almost one-quarter (23%) normally work directly with the machine translation vendor.

For which vendors and/or tools marketers are currently using for their machine translation/ localization needs, almost half (46%) use Google Translate/Google Translate API, one-third (33%) use Bing Microsoft Translator/Microsoft Translator API and three in ten (30%) are using OpenAI/ ChatGPT.

Over one in five marketers (22%) are using AWS/Amazon for their machine translation/ localization needs, one in five are using LibreTranslate (19%) and Rozetta T-400 (19%) while smaller numbers are using Yandex (18%), DeepL (14%), ModernMT (13%) and Mirai (10%).
Marketers in France (16%) and Germany (29%) are more likely than those in Japan (4%) and the US (7%) to say they are using DeepL.
Over three-quarters of marketers (77%) say they have used an AI-assisted writing tool for any of their content while one in five (21%) have not, but have thought of doing so.
Marketers in Japan (93%), the US (87%) and France (83%) are more likely than marketers in Germany (47%) to say they have used an AI-assisted writing tool for their content.
But, half of German marketers (50%) have thought about it.

Looking ahead 2-3 years, almost all marketers (97%) say it is likely that a large amount of content for business will be generated by AI-assisted writing with over two in five (42%) saying this will be very likely.

0nouns%20and%20branded%20terms%0ACapitalize:%0A-%20**Help%20Center**%0A-%20**Privacy%20Policy**%0A-%20**Terms%20&%20Conditions**%0A%0A###%20Quotation%20and%20capitalization%0AWhen%20modifying%20capitalization%20within%20quotes,%20use%20brackets:%0A-%20Correct:%20TechCrunch%20notes%20DeepL%E2%80%99s%20fortunate%20position,%20as%20%E2%80%9C%5Ba%5D%20lot%20of%20startups%20have%20been%20struggling.%E2%80%9D%0A%0A##%20Word%20list%0A%0A-%20**Cancel**:%20Follow%20American%20English%20spelling%20(e.g.,%20**canceled**,%20not%20**cancelled**).%0A-%20**DeepL%20Translate**:%20Use%20only%20for%20SEO%20purposes;%20otherwise,%20use%20**DeepL%20Translator**.%0A-%20**Subscribe**:%20Refers%20to%20the%20process%20of%20upgrading%20to%20DeepL%20Pro.%0A%0A##%20Copywriting%20aspects%0A%0A###%20Keep%20it%20short%0AEven%20small%20amounts%20of%20English%20copy%20may%20require%20more%20space%20in%20other%20languages.%0A-%20Translation%20results%20%E2%86%92%20Translations%0A-%20Desktop%20apps%20%E2%86%92%20Apps%0A%0A##%20Writing%20for%20error%20messages%0A%0A-%20Be%20clear%20and%20identify%20the%20main%20issue.%0A-%20Avoid%20blaming%20the%20user.%0A-%20Provide%20a%20solution%20or%20next%20step.%0A%0A##%20Writing%20for%20accessibility%0A%0AFor%20practical%20tips%20on%20writing%20for%20screen%20readers,%20alt%20texts,%20and%20ARIA%20labels,%20see%20the%20DeepL%20Accessibility%20Guide.%0A%0A---%0A%0A##%20References%0A-%20The%20American%20Heritage%20Dictionary:%20%5Bahdictionary.com%5D(https://ahdictionary.com)%0A-%20The%20Chicago%20Manual%20of%20Style:%20%5Bchicagomanualofstyle.org%5D(https://www.chicagomanualofstyle.org)%0A-%20Oxford%20Dictionary:%20%5Blexico.com%5D(https://www.lexico.com/en/definition/color)%0A-%20Merriam-Webster%20Dictionary:%20%5Bmerriam-webster.com%5D(https://www.merriam-webster.com)%0A-%20Apple%20Style%20Guide:%20%5Bhelp.apple.com%5D(https://help.apple.com/applestyleguide)
